stem: A logistics company's private subnets in AZ-A and AZ-B both lost internet access when the single NAT gateway in AZ-A failed, because AZ-B's route table also pointed its default route at that same NAT gateway.

choices.text: Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance in AZ-A, but keep referencing it from both AZs' route tables
Move both AZs' private subnets onto the VPC's main route table, pointed at the AZ-A NAT gateway
Create one NAT gateway per AZ and point each AZ's route table only at its own AZ's NAT gateway
Add a second NAT gateway in AZ-A for redundancy within that same AZ

rationale: Creating one NAT gateway per AZ and pointing each AZ's route table only at its own AZ's NAT gateway removes the cross-AZ dependency entirely, so a NAT gateway failure in one AZ no longer affects the other AZ's outbound path. Swapping the NAT gateway for a NAT instance in AZ-A but still referencing it from both AZs' route tables changes the technology but not the architecture: AZ-B's traffic still depends on a single resource that lives only in AZ-A, so the same outage would recur. Consolidating both AZs onto the VPC's main route table pointed at the AZ-A NAT gateway makes the dependency more explicit, not less, since every subnet in both AZs now shares one entry. Adding a second NAT gateway in AZ-A only protects against one NAT gateway failing inside that AZ; AZ-B's traffic would still be routed out through AZ-A, so losing AZ-A itself would still take down AZ-B's internet path.
